A vignette to help understand how to use PsyR to enact the Scheffé technique, which uses an ANOVA F Simultaneous Test Procedure and a Scheffé Simultaneous Confidence Interval (SCI) method for making inferences for multiple contrasts [@bird2004]. This method is appropriate when participants are randomly allocated, and only 1 Independent Variable (with J levels) is present.

Engaging in a Scheffé post-hoc contrasts analysis using SCIs enables a researcher to make inferences of greater specificity than other approaches. Specifically, SCIs allow for inferences regarding the magnitude of the effect captured by a contrast. This is achieved while holding the FWER below ⍺, as the Scheffé method controls the FWER for the set of all conceivable contrasts (when J \> 2). However, the flexibility this method affords comes at the cost of power, especially when compared to a planned contrasts analysis investigating only a few contrasts of interest chosen a priori to data collection. 


```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

## The Packages

To use PsyR to calculate confidence intervals over contrast effects, we will utilise a workflow with functions from [afex](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/afex/versions/1.4-1) to implement ANOVA models, and [emmeans](https://rvlenth.github.io/emmeans/) to obtain estimated marginal means and the required contrast estimates. So let's load those packages, and any others that are helpful for our workflow.


```{r, loadpackages, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(afex)
library(emmeans)
library(ggplot2)
library(PsyR)
library(tidyverse)
```

## The Data

Lets load the data, then call the `head()` function to print the first 5 rows.

```{r loaddata}
data(fatigue)
head(fatigue, 5) %>%
  knitr::kable(format = "html", table.attr = "style='width:50%;'")
```

Have you forgotten the details of the fatigue dataframe? Call the help function using `?df` to open its documentation.


```{r, whatfatigue, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, eval = FALSE}
?fatigue
```

When working with this dataframe, we need the independent variables to be represented as factors (rather than doubles). So, call `factor()` reassign the "Group" column to the factor datatype, and to relabel the levels of the driver fatigue independent variable.


```{r sortfatigue}
fatigue <- fatigue %>%
  mutate(
    Group = factor(
      Group,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4),
      labels = c("Alert", "Mild", "Moderate", "Extreme")
    )
  )
```

Time to plot our data, with help from the ggplot2 package.

Using a pipe, lets tell `ggplot()` to take in the fatigue dataset (the one we just edited, with the better labels). Then, within `aes()` lets create a canvas with "Group" on the X axis and "Errors" on the Y axis. Lets also colour-code our four groups by calling fill: [Alert]{style="color: OrangeRed;"}, [Mild]{style="color: OliveDrab;"}, [Moderate]{style="color: CadetBlue;"} and [Extreme]{style="color: DarkOrchid;"}.

Next, lets create a boxplot using `geom_boxplot()` and make it look nice and clean using `theme_classic()`.

```{r boxplotit, fig.width = 7.1, fig.height = 4}
fatigue %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Group, y = Errors, fill = Group)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_classic(base_size = 14)
```

## The Analysis

Lets prepare to run some statistical tests!

Here we will create the building blocks of our eventual ANOVA output. First, lets create a new object labelled *mod* (short for model). Call the `aov_ez()` function which takes in the "id" column to identify subjects, the "Errors" column as the dependent variable, the fatigue dataframe, and the "Group" column set as between-subjects. This aggregates across our Group column, so it isn't useful on its own.

Next, lets create a new object *emms* (short for estimated marginal means) calling the `emmeans()` function and specifying that we want to take in *mod* (the object we just made) and output based upon "Group". Now we are heading in the right direction, as our results are split by factor ("Alert", "Mild", "Moderate", "Extreme").

```{r, aov}
# perform the statistical model
mod <- aov_ez(
  "id",
  "Errors",
  fatigue,
  between = "Group"
)
emms <- emmeans(mod, "Group")
knitr::kable(emms, digits = 3)
```

Time to define our contrasts!

Lets create an object called *between_contrasts*. Next, call the `list()` function and define our four contrasts of interest. The contrasts represent the following:

- "Fatigue-Alert" - The difference between the average of fatigued conditions and the alert condition

- "Extreme-Mod, Mild" - The difference between Extreme fatigue and the average of Moderate and Mild fatigue.

- "Low-High" - The difference between the average of Alert and Mild fatigue versus the average of Moderate and Extreme fatigue.

- "Alert-Mild" - The difference between the Alert and Mild fatigue conditions.

```{r definecontrasts}
between_contrasts = list(
  "Fatigue-Alert" = c(-1, 1/3, 1/3, 1/3),
  "Extreme-Mod, Mild" = c(0, -1/2, -1/2, 1),
  "Low-High" = c(1/2, 1/2, -1/2, -1/2),
  "Alert-Mild" = c(1, -1, 0, 0)
)
```

Now that we have defined our contrasts, lets create our ANOVA table. Create the *btwn_fx* object, then call the `contrast()` function from the emmeans package, setting *emms* in the "object" argument and *between_contrasts* in the "method" argument (which will take in our newly defined contrasts).

```{r, between_fx}
btwn_fx <- contrast(emms, between_contrasts)
knitr::kable(btwn_fx, digits = 3)
```

Finally, lets calculate some confidence intervals to estimate effect sizes. Lets create the list *contrasts_w_cis* using the `psyci()` function, specifying the following:

- The model is the previously made *mod* object, where the model must be made using the afex package - afex_aov

- The contrast_tables argument is set as the previously made *btwn_fx*

- The family list is set as "b", specifying that the contrast table is between-subjects. The family_list must take in a list of the same length as contrast_tables.

- The between_factors argument takes in a list of between subjects factor names, as previously defined in the "Group" object.

- Alpha is set at 0.05 (both here and by default), indicating the desired type I error rate. 

```{r, psyci}
contrasts_w_cis <- psyci(
  model = mod,
  contrast_tables = list(btwn_fx),
  family_list = list("b"),
  method = "ph",
  alpha = .05,
  between_factors = list("Group")
)
knitr::kable(contrasts_w_cis, digits = 3)
```

## The Interpretation

There is evidence of significant differences in the "Fatigue-Alert", "Extreme-Mod, Mild", and "Low-Hi" contrasts (p \< 0.05).

- Compared to alert drivers, having any level of fatigue results in between 2.877 and 9.123 more driving errors.

- Drivers with extreme fatigue make between 4.187 and 10.813 more errors than the average of Moderate and Mild fatigue conditions.

- Drivers with low fatigue (the average of alert and mild conditions) make between 4.295 and 9.705 fewer errors than those with high fatigue (the average of moderate and extreme conditions)
